title: Diagonalisation: Eigenvectors as Natural Axes
topic: A 2×2 matrix maps the unit circle to an ellipse. The two directions that stretch without rotating are the eigenvectors; their stretch factors are the eigenvalues. In the eigenbasis A is diagonal: A = P D P⁻¹.

beats.narration: Apply a matrix to every point on the unit circle. What comes out?

elements.content: A circle, a matrix, an ellipse — and two stubborn axes.

beats.narration: Start with the unit circle, and pick a matrix — say A equals two, one, one, two.

elements.content: Unit circle radius 1 in amber, persistent
12-24 sample points on the unit circle in amber-400
Matrix card 'A = [[2,1],[1,2]]' violet/teal columns, on backdrop panel

beats.narration: Send every point through A. The circle becomes an ellipse. Most directions tilt as they stretch.

elements.content: Animated morph: each sample point moves from unit-circle position p to Ap, tracing the deformation in ~2-3s
Resulting ellipse, semi-major 3 along (1,1)/√2, semi-minor 1 along (1,-1)/√2, dashed amber-300 outline

beats.narration: But two directions are stubborn — they only stretch, they don't rotate. These are the eigenvectors, and their stretch factors are the eigenvalues lambda one and lambda two.

elements.content: Eigenvector v₁ = (1,1)/√2 violet, with shadow showing where (1,1) lands after A: at λ₁·(1,1)/√2 = 3 × that direction
Eigenvector v₂ = (1,-1)/√2 teal — fixed (λ₂ = 1, vector unchanged)
Two long dashed lines along the eigenvector directions — the natural axes

beats.narration: Use them as a new basis. In those coordinates, A is just diagonal — pure stretching along the axes.

elements.content: Centred 'A = P D P⁻¹' decomposition with P, D = diag(3,1), P⁻¹ panels — D in violet/teal columns

beats.narration: Hard problems become easy in the right basis.

elements.content: 'Eigenvectors are the natural axes.' huge serif italic, 'natural axes' in amber-300
'A acts diagonally in its own coordinates.' subtitle
